column3: Near-verbatim parallel: gratitude benefits its bearer, while disbelief leaves God self-sufficient.
Links divine bounty to gratitude, though it lacks the focus's immediate test of possession.
Commands David's household to enact gratitude amid granted power, closely framing Solomon's response.
Immediate alternative transport claim supplies the same throne, deadline, and capability contrast.
Immediate prompt for the throne's delivery sets up the focus's completed transport.
Directly joins gratitude and disbelief to the recipient's outcome while God remains independent.
Its possessor of knowledge from the Book closely echoes the focus's agent, in a different scene.
Solomon's prayer for gratitude after favor is the local precursor to his interpretation here.
Shares only the language of a settled outcome, here in punitive rather than gifted possession.
Moon observation and Abraham's guidance inquiry do not clarify the throne, test, or gratitude.
Direct local parallel: divine favor is set against the majority's ingratitude.
Its generic settling of every affair only faintly echoes the throne's stable arrival.
Guidance benefiting its recipient parallels the focus's claim that gratitude returns to oneself.
Explicitly makes worship of God issue in gratitude, matching the focus's proper response to favor.
A wretched permanent abode supplies only a punitive contrast to the focus's settled throne.
States that guidance and error return to each person, paralleling the focus's self-directed consequence.
The later altered throne is explicitly used to test the queen's recognition within the same episode.
Defines created order as a test that discloses conduct, directly supporting the focus's trial reading.
Mercy obscured from Noah's people does not clarify the focus's knowledge, favor, or gratitude.
The queen's prior worship and disbelief form the later outcome of the throne episode's test.
Provision is requested so its recipients may be grateful, a clear but differently situated parallel.
Effort benefits its bearer and God needs nothing, closely matching the focus's self-benefit and sufficiency.
Judgment exposes what each self sent ahead, supporting the focus's disclosure-through-test motif.
Treats disbelief as covering divine favor under God's total ownership, without the focus's concrete test.
A ruler's God-given kingship becomes arrogant self-claim, a distant contrast to Solomon's attribution.
The delivered throne leads the queen to recognition of prior knowledge and submission in the same narrative.
Deliverance is called a great test, supplying a broad precedent for favor as examination.
Its unreturning gaze is a negative visual echo, not the focus's rapid delivery or gratitude.
Calling a people tested is a local but unrelated use of the testing theme.
Restricted gazes in paradise do not illuminate the focus's returned glance or stable throne.
Its unbelief clause affirms that God is independent of all worlds, but omits gratitude's self-benefit.
Strength and trustworthiness loosely characterize the prior transport claimant, without explaining the focus.
Divine bounty and contentment offer a limited gratitude context without the focus's testing structure.
Self-sufficiency claimed by a person sharply contrasts with the focus's attribution to the self-sufficient Lord.
Prayer, almsgiving, and certainty in the Hereafter do not clarify the throne event or its test.
The self-sufficient pose contrasts with the focus's insistence that true sufficiency belongs to God.
Knowledge of the Book is a distant lexical context, not an account of the focus's knowledgeable agent.
Relocates apparent human agency to God and calls the event a good test, broadly paralleling the focus.
The accusation of ingratitude turns patronage into political control, a limited contrast to grateful attribution.
Its command to disbelieve supplies only a general negative counterpart to the focus's gratitude choice.
The queen's letter and awaited reply establish the diplomatic sequence that precedes the throne request.
Promises divine bounty beyond a lost income source and affirms divine sufficiency, in a different setting.
Calling mercy one's own is a direct ethical contrast to Solomon's attribution of the throne to his Lord.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it, supplying the focus's negative response to favor.
Generic disbelief and future knowledge do not materially develop the focus's gift or test.
Its bad permanent abode is only a contrastive use of settled dwelling.
The command that immediately precedes the throne request supplies the narrative escalation behind it.
A provisional account of the lasting abode has only a remote relation to the focus's settled object.
Protection is explicitly a reward for gratitude, reinforcing gratitude's consequential benefit.
Angels praise their Lord around the throne, providing a broad throne-and-gratitude frame.
Describes divine favor as a freely given gift reaching new recipients, supporting the favor side of the test.
The mountain scene tests the limits of sight and endurance, not the focus's gifted throne or gratitude.
The punishment of Lot's people has no explanatory link to the focus's throne episode.
Turning away and disbelieving gives only a general negative counterpart to gratitude for favor.
The women's reaction to Joseph's appearance does not clarify the focus's observation or trial.
Deviation from signs and punishment do not clarify the throne transport or gratitude response.
A changed dwelling after a slip offers only a remote contrast to the focus's stable placement.
The inherited Book is a prior divine gift that makes recipients responsible, broadly supporting favor as trial.
Moses's search for fire belongs to an unrelated local scene and does not explain the focus.
Near-verbatim parallel: gratitude is for oneself, while God remains rich and praiseworthy despite disbelief.
A second sighting has no semantic connection to the throne's arrival, favor, or gratitude.
Directly presents people exchanging God's favor for disbelief, the negative side of the focus's test.
Granted security and authority are tested through worship rather than disbelief, closely paralleling favor's trial.
What God gives becomes a test of conduct, a direct but more general counterpart to the focus's trial.
The queen's final recognition and submission complete the narrative in which the focus's throne sign operates.
Saba receives abundant provision and is commanded to be grateful, linking the queen's people to the focus's theme.
Its demand for evidence and inherited knowledge only distantly echoes the focus's knowledge-from-the-Book phrase.
Deferring to God and the Messenger has no substantive connection to the throne or gratitude test.
Calls Abraham's ordeal a manifest test, providing a concise general parallel to the focus's trial.
A good permanent abode only contrastively echoes the focus's settled throne.
The rescue of the believers in another local account does not clarify the focus's event.
Warning to disbelievers supplies a broad negative outcome for the focus's gratitude-versus-disbelief choice.
A clear sighting on the horizon does not illuminate the focus's transport or ethical response.
The Book's descent from the Mighty, Wise One offers only a distant Book-knowledge context.
God's ownership of all things is joined to His self-sufficiency and praise-worthiness, directly framing the focus's conclusion.
Testing possessions and persons is a broad parallel without the focus's favor-and-gratitude logic.
Seeking God's favor while supporting His cause shows bounty generating responsible action, though not the throne test.
God's appreciative reward for good deeds is a limited parallel to the focus's gratitude motif.
Divine exclusive knowledge is too general to explain the focus's particular knowledge-from-the-Book agent.
Selfless hospitality contrasts possessiveness, but does not clarify the focus's gratitude or transported throne.
Placement in a secure resting place is a distant biological echo of the focus's stable arrival.
Its christological disbelief and worship command do not materially clarify the focus's test of favor.
Generic denial provides only a minimal negative counterpart to the focus's gratitude/disbelief alternatives.
Concealing testimony and disputing inherited identities do not explain the focus's knowledge or favor.
Disbelief in signs is a broad negative pole, without the focus's possession, test, or self-benefit.
The better permanent dwelling in paradise only contrastively recalls the focus's settled object.
Wealth and children cannot make one self-sufficient before God, supporting the focus's divine-sufficiency distinction.
God's expansive favor replacing apostates is a remote parallel without the focus's gratitude response.
Mercy, pursuit of divine bounty, and gratitude form a direct thematic parallel in a different sign.
Bounty is linked to charity and good returned to oneself, but the focus's test is not developed.
Detailed pilgrimage rules have no explanatory relation to the throne, gratitude, or divine sufficiency.
Signs also test those who receive them, directly supporting the focus's interpretation of the throne event.
Resurrection and accounting for deeds offer only a remote consequence for disbelief.
Temporary benefit followed by punishment for disbelief reinforces the focus's warning against covering divine favor.
Desired fruit in paradise does not clarify any component of the focus ayah.
Those enriched by divine favor respond with resentment and disbelief, a direct negative counterpart to Solomon's gratitude.
Household-entry etiquette does not clarify the focus's favor, trial, or throne scene.
It explicitly presents the human response as gratitude or ingratitude after being shown the way.
Exclusive worship and warning of punishment offer only a general backdrop to disbelief.
God's favor and mercy interrupt deserved punishment, supporting the focus's account of unowed divine favor.
Revival after death is expressly given so its recipients may be grateful, linking favor to response.
Commands gratitude without disbelief, directly supplying the focus's central response contrast.
Permitted provision is followed by the command to thank God, a clear favor-and-gratitude parallel.
God's bounty toward people is contrasted with widespread ingratitude.
God grants kingship, knowledge, and bodily capacity, closely framing bestowed authority and knowledge.
David receives kingship, wisdom, and taught knowledge from God, a direct power-and-gift parallel.
God gives and removes dominion and grants good, framing royal power as bestowed rather than owned.
All bounty is in God's hand and given to whom He wills, supporting Solomon's attribution of favor.
God rewards the grateful, reinforcing the consequential value of gratitude.
Sending and teaching through the Messenger is called a great divine favor, linking knowledge and gift.
God grants Abraham's family the Book, wisdom, and great dominion, a close knowledge-and-kingship parallel.
God's favor includes teaching from the Book and wisdom, directly framing knowledge as an unowed gift.
Gratitude and faith are set against punishment while God is appreciative and knowing.
A commanded remembrance of God's protective favor supplies a concrete response to received help.
Moses recalls God's favors of prophets, kings, and gifts not given to others.
God tests some people through others, supporting the focus's reading of an event as examination.
God raises whom He wills in degrees while remaining wise and knowing, broadly framing granted distinction.
Settlement on earth and provision are explicitly followed by the charge of little gratitude.
Satan's stated aim that most will not be grateful supplies the focus's negative ethical pole.
Settlement, land, and built dwellings are tied to remembering God's favors.
Rescue, shelter, support, and provision are explicitly given so believers may be grateful.
God's favor is tied to people's response and change within themselves, clarifying favor's moral stakes.
God's bounty and mercy are named as the proper ground of rejoicing.
God gives each possessor of merit His bounty, supporting the focus's account of bestowed favor.
A person receiving mercy after hardship claims evils gone and becomes boastful, contrasting Solomon's gratitude.
Joseph is given judgment and knowledge as a divine reward, paralleling gifted knowledge.
God raises whom He wills in degrees and places knowledge above knowledge, framing the focus's learned agent.
Near-direct parallel: gratitude brings increase, while ingratitude brings severe consequence.
God gives beyond human counting, framing the throne as part of unexhausted divine favor.
Abraham praises God for bestowed sons, modeling grateful attribution for a received gift.
Created means of travel and provision are given so people may seek bounty and be grateful.
Human inability to count God's favors reinforces the focus's attribution of the throne to divine grace.
Every favor is from God, directly grounding Solomon's statement that the throne is from his Lord's bounty.
Disbelief in what has been given supplies the negative response to the focus's gratitude test.
Family and provision are called God's favors before their denial is condemned.
Created faculties and received knowledge culminate in the expectation of gratitude.
Enjoying lawful provision is explicitly conditioned by gratitude to God.
Abraham is named grateful for God's favors and is then chosen and guided.
Noah is identified as a grateful servant, furnishing a prophetic model of gratitude.
God makes ships move so people may seek His bounty, linking power and provision to divine mercy.
Rescue from harm followed by turning away gives a concrete negative counterpart to grateful attribution.
Human honor and good provision form a broad frame of divine favor.
A person turns away when favored and calls intensely under hardship, contrasting stable gratitude.
The garden owner is told to attribute possession to God rather than claim it as self-made.
Good provision is given with a warning against abuse, preserving the accountability of received bounty.
David and Solomon are both given judgment and knowledge, directly contextualizing Solomon's granted capacity.
God teaches David a useful craft and asks whether people will be grateful.
The wind and other forces are subjected to Solomon by divine command, framing exceptional capacity as gift.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are bestowed while people are said to give little thanks.
God's favor and mercy avert punishment, supporting the focus's description of grace as unowed.
Immediate Solomon context: David and Solomon receive knowledge and praise God for His favor.
Solomon's inherited rule and taught knowledge of creature speech establish the gifted capacity behind the episode.
Solomon rejects the queen's gift by distinguishing what God gave him from their wealth, immediately preceding the throne request.
Provision is sought from God and joined to worship and gratitude.
Mercy after harm is followed by association, a direct negative counterpart to grateful recognition of favor.
Disbelief in what God has given directly states the focus's negative response to bounty.
God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life, grounding the focus's attribution of effective power to God.
God lavishes outward and inward favors while some dispute without knowledge, Book, or light.
Bestowed hearing, sight, and hearts are followed by the charge of little gratitude.
David receives divine favor and extraordinary service, closely paralleling Solomon's gifted royal setting.
The ungrateful are singled out for recompense, reinforcing the focus's gratitude-versus-disbelief consequence.
Divine bounty is extended or restricted while most people fail to recognize it.
God extends provision and replaces what is spent, framing bounty as divine rather than self-originated.
Commands remembrance of God's favor and asks whether any creator besides God provides.
The people of Paradise praise God for removing grief, showing praise as the response to completed favor.
Provisioned fruit is followed by the direct question of whether people will give thanks.
A granted favor is claimed as personal knowledge and then named a test, directly contrasting the focus's grateful reading.
Night and day are made for rest and sight as divine favor, yet most people are ungrateful.
God forms people and provides good things, then is praised as Lord of the worlds.
When favor is bestowed, a person turns away; hardship reverses this conduct, sharply contrasting gratitude.
Settling upon a mount leads to remembering the Lord's favor and glorifying Him, closely echoing settled possession and response.
The sea is subjected so people may seek divine bounty and be grateful.
The prayer explicitly asks for ability to thank God's favor and to act righteously.
God is self-sufficient while people are needy; turning away leads to replacement, directly supporting the focus's conclusion.
The repeated challenge over which divine favors are denied provides a concentrated gratitude-and-denial frame.
Fresh water is a divine mercy followed by the question of why people are not grateful.
Wealth and children are explicitly called a trial, closely matching possession as an examination.
Earth is made manageable and provision is granted, framing received capacity and sustenance as divine gift.
The garden owners are expressly tested through entrusted abundance, a close possession-as-trial parallel.
Commands public acknowledgment of the Lord's favor, directly modeling the focus's attribution of grace.
